newsitem.title: UK: British money supply growth rings inflation bells.
newsitem.headline: British money supply growth rings inflation bells.

text.p: British broad money supply grew strongly again in March, fuelling concerns that inflationary pressures are building as consumers and companies appear to be borrowing and spending freely.

The Bank of England on Friday said broad money supply (M4) grew by 11.2 percent in the year to March, unchanged from February's growth rate and still well above the upper limit of the government's three to nine percent monitoring range.
Total lending by banks and building societies rose by 4.5 billion pounds ($7.3 billion), lower than February's 8.2 billion rise.

City economists, who had been expecting a slight slowdown in the growth rate of M4, said the series was in keeping with a batch of economic activity data out this week showing robust growth and possible early signs of inflationary pressures.
"The M4 figures, along with the labour market data, are the source of upside risk to inflation," said Alex Garrard, UK economist at UBS.

He said the Bank of England would use it to strengthen its case for an interest rate rise. "The Bank is unlikely to change its advice to an incoming Chancellor -- it will continue to press fairly strongly for a rate rise."

The Bank has already voiced its concern about the strength of M4 to Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke. It wants to see an immediate rise in the key base rate from the present 6.0 percent to head of inflationary pressures.

Broad money supply comprises all notes and coins held by the public, along with bank and building society accounts. It is considered to be a leading indicator for inflation, although its record is patchy and the lead times are long and variable.

The figures have been distorted over the last year or so by technical changes to the British money markets which have swollen the totals. But even stripped of these effects, analysts said it was still above the government's monitoring range and had been since October 1995.
This and other strong economic data meant the inflation target would not be met in medium term unless interest rates rise, they said.

"M4, along with most other figures, is pointing upwards and growth at this sort of level is in the long run inconsistent with the 2.5 inflation target," said David Philpotts, UK economist at Schroders.
Figures out on Thursday showed British underlying inflation fell to 2.7 percent in March from 2.9 percent in February, just above the target.
While falling commodity prices and the strong pound mean high street prices may fall further in the next few months, other figures showed pressures starting to build.
The labour market report on Wednesday said average earnings grew by five percent in the year to February, and business surveys in the past month reported skills shortages in the services area.
The central bank will be able to put its case for higher rates to the next Chancellor of the Exchequer on May 7, just days after the May 1 election.

If the opinion polls prove accurate opposition Labour Party's finance spokesman Gordon Brown will sit across the table from Bank Governor Eddie George instead of the ruling Conservative's Kenneth Clarke.

Philpotts said Brown had the greater incentive to raise rates at that meeting. "Clarke has already earned credibility with financial markets that he is tough on inflation. Brown hasn't and an interest rate rise early on is an easy and quick way to do that."

Other figures out on Friday showed the housing market recovery continuing, but at an unspectacular rate. The Building Societies Association said societies approved home loans worth 3.256 billion pounds compared with 3.359 billion in February.

"The figures demonstrate the recovery in the housing market is still on track," said Adrian Coles, Director General of the BSA. "It is worth noting, however, that the recovery remains moderate, and that spring is traditionally a time when the housing market picks up." ($ = 0.612 British Pounds)
